title: Replying to @Antony Also I heard the Broadway cast named the puppet a...
transcript: okay so imagine you're watching the King Kong musical on Broadway and it's terrible but that enormous King Kong puppet is the coolest thing you've ever seen in your goddamn life and just when you thought the novelty was wearing off toward the end of Act 2 they pull out a very simple but clever trick of staging to send chills down your spine and make your heart skip a beat welcome to another episode of Overthinking Theatre Throwback where I do retrospectives on pieces of recent theatre history that I don't think get enough attention so the King Kong musical had a bit of a rough road to Broadway it premiered in Australia in 2013 and by the time it got to Broadway [in 2018] it was a completely different musical and I mean that quite literally like they actually scrapped the entire book and score and cycled through multiple different creative teams to help write it from scratch fun fact Jason Robert Brown was actually attached to write the score at one point but they ended up landing on Eddie Perfect who also wrote the Beetlejuice musical but the one thing that remained was the puppet and what a puppet it was! at 20 feet tall and weighing a ton it was operated by a mix of cables, animatronics, and a team of onstage puppeteers and I found it so impressive that I actually think it made a strong case for telling this story in the medium of live theatre did the show need to have songs in it? no not at all in fact this is one of the few cases in recent memory of a new Broadway musical that didn't even get a cast recording was the script any good? no of course not it was written by Jack Thorne god don't get me started on him but for me it still kind of worked as a piece of live theatre because the effect of King Kong as a character is that he is this imposing, awesome wonder to behold and here he is not on a screen but right there in the room with you but maybe just as importantly the puppetry wasn't just impressive in terms of its scale like they really brought him to life as a character even his face was articulated with animatronics so there was emotion in his eyes and you could get that pathos for this tragic figure but you might be asking if the puppet is so huge and required all this rigging and all these puppeteers how did they replicate the big, climactic moment where he breaks free from his chains? do they somehow get the puppet to fly over the audience like in Spider Man? no what they did do was a lot simpler but maybe all the more thrilling because of it so you don't really notice this throughout the performance but the puppet spends most of its time upstage kind of removed back from the audience but in the scene where he breaks free they rig him up to a new cable downstage that allows him to come right up to the edge of the stage and it's only a difference of a few meters like you wouldn't think it would make that big of a difference but it really, really did cause suddenly he's right there and he's looking at us and he kind of sniffs us and looks around and then lets out this big roar at us and you could feel the tension in the audience there was a lot of murmuring and nervous giggling and I wasn't even that close I was maybe toward the back of the orchestra but I was all tense and holding my breath and my eyes were super wide and it's a good lesson that you don't have to make something super immersive to show an understanding of how to use physical space as a storytelling tool in theatre and I won't defend a single other thing about this show but being in the room with that puppet was unforgettable so where is the puppet now? I wish I knew! in the middle of filming this I decided to send a general inquiry to the company that created the puppet I'm sure they don't own it but they might know what happened to it so I'll let you know if they respond
classificationReason: Reply/throwback video about the King Kong Broadway musical (2018), which is not on the list. Beetlejuice is only mentioned in passing as another Eddie Perfect credit.
